messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 53
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Painter
  trauma_type: Civilian in war zone
  pcl5: 34

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Loss of Control: Lack of control, Auditory (Explosion): Explosion or bang sounds
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rumination: Meaning: go over and over why the event happened to me, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Avoid News: News reports about events similar to what happened to me
  Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people, Body on Alert: My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Meaning: Nothing in my life feels meaningful anymore, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajan had been painting houses in the same Boston suburb for over twenty years, a trade he had learned from his father after immigrating from Gujarat. His life had been one of quiet, steady rhythms—the smell of fresh paint, the scrape of a brush, the satisfaction of a finished room. That ended on a Tuesday afternoon in September, three years ago, when he had stopped at a market in a busy plaza. A delivery truck backfired, and a split second later, a man near the entrance dropped a heavy metal tray. The sound was a flat, percussive crack that seemed to come from everywhere at once. For Rajan, the world collapsed into a single, frozen moment. He was no longer in the plaza; he was back in the narrow alley behind his uncle’s shop in Ahmedabad, pinned against a wall as mortar fire rained down around him. He had been twenty-three, a civilian caught in a crossfire he had spent thirty years trying to forget. In the plaza, he had dropped to his knees, his hands over his ears, his body locked in a tight, protective curl, just as it had been in that alley. When the memory came, it was not a story he told himself; it was a physical reenactment. He felt the grit of the alley wall against his back, the crushing weight of his own body trying to disappear. And with that memory came a wave of grief so profound it stole his breath—grief for the boy he had been, for the uncle who had died that day, for the life of simple meaning he had built since.

In the weeks that followed, the world rearranged itself around that sound. A car door slamming in the street, a child dropping a book in the library, the clatter of a paint can in his own truck—each one could trigger the same visceral plunge. He had come to believe that the world was a fundamentally dangerous place, that safety was an illusion he could no longer afford. The market, the plaza, the busy intersections he had once navigated without thought—these became zones of constant threat. He began to work harder at keeping busy, taking on double shifts, painting through lunch, filling every silent moment with the scrape of a roller or the hum of a radio. What frightened him most was the stillness, because in stillness the memories came. He would find himself in a quiet room, and suddenly his body would lock into that same frozen crouch, his muscles braced for an impact that never came. He was certain he was no longer capable of doing the things that had defined him—of being the calm, reliable father and husband his family knew. Nothing in his life felt meaningful anymore; the satisfaction he had once taken in a clean, straight line of paint had evaporated. He had started to avoid the news, switching off the television whenever reports mentioned conflict or violence, because those images fed the loop. He would ruminate for hours, going over and over why the event had happened to him, why he had survived when his uncle had not, as if finding an answer might undo the memory.

The causal connections tightened into a relentless cycle. The triggers—the bang of a door, the crack of a dropped tool—would instantly activate his threat system, leaving him hypervigilant, his body constantly tense and ready to react. His wife noticed he jumped at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people. He was always on guard, scanning rooms for exits, watching people’s hands. This state of threat made the memories more accessible; when he was already tense, the flashbacks came more easily, and they brought with them the overwhelming grief. That grief, in turn, reinforced his belief that the world was dangerous and his life meaningless, which made him even more vigilant. His avoidance strategies—the frantic busyness, the refusal to watch the news—were intended to control the triggers, but they had the opposite effect. By never allowing himself to process the event, the memory remained raw and extreme, so hard to believe it had actually happened to him. The more he avoided, the more potent the triggers became. A single smell, like the diesel exhaust from a delivery truck, could send him into a full reenactment, his body locked in that same position, his mind lost in the past. The threat state made him hypervigilant to new triggers, which meant he was constantly scanning for sounds, and those sounds would trigger the memory again. The memory, in turn, fed his negative appraisals, deepening his conviction that he was no longer capable and that the world was a dangerous place. These appraisals made the triggers feel more imminent, more personal, more inevitable.

He had stopped taking jobs in busy commercial areas, telling his boss he preferred residential work. He avoided the plaza entirely. He began to feel his body constantly tense, even at home, even in bed. The cycle had ground down his marriage; his wife felt she was living with a stranger who flinched at her touch. What finally brought Rajan to seek help was a moment in his own kitchen, when his daughter dropped a glass. The shattering sound sent him to the floor, his hands over his head, his breath ragged, and he could not get up for several minutes. He was terrified that he was losing his mind. He was most afraid that he would never feel safe again, but he was also, quietly, hoping that someone might help him find a way to live with the memory without being consumed by it.
